question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A giraffe has twice as many neck bones as us|An octopus has three hearts|A snail has thousands of tiny teeth|A butterfly tastes with its feet
explanation: A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as a person. Each one is just very long. The other three are true.
hintText: A long neck needs long bones. Does it need more of them?

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Sound cannot travel through empty space|The Moon shows us a new side each night|A day on Mars is about as long as ours|Venus takes longer to spin once than to orbit
explanation: The Moon always turns the same side to the Earth. Nobody saw its far side until a spacecraft photographed it in 1959. The other three are true.
hintText: Think of the Moon's face on different nights. Does the pattern on it change?

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Fingernails grow faster than toenails|Your stomach lining renews every few days|You cannot breathe and swallow at once|A grown-up has more bones than a baby
explanation: A baby has between 270 and 300 bones, many of them still soft. Many grow together, and an adult has 206. The other three are true.
hintText: Bones can grow together over the years.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A hummingbird can fly backwards|An ostrich hides its head in the sand|A cow's stomach has four parts|Sea otters wrap up in seaweed to sleep
explanation: An ostrich lays its neck flat on the ground to hide, and it turns its eggs in a nest dug in the sand. From far away the head seems gone. The other three are true.
hintText: One of these is an old saying, not something anyone has seen.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: The Pacific is wider than the Moon|The Sahara is mostly made of sand dunes|Antarctica is a desert|There is gold dissolved in sea water
explanation: Only about a quarter of the Sahara is sand. Most of it is bare rock and gravel. The other three are true.
hintText: A desert is a dry place. It does not have to be sandy, or even hot.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A peanut is a relative of the pea|Honey can keep for thousands of years|Purple carrots are older than orange ones|White chocolate has the most cocoa powder
explanation: White chocolate has no cocoa powder at all. It is made from cocoa butter, the fat of the bean, with milk and sugar. The other three are true.
hintText: Cocoa powder is dark brown.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A day has 86,400 seconds|A billion seconds is about 32 years|A year has more than a million minutes|A week has 10,080 minutes
explanation: A year has 525,600 minutes: 60 × 24 × 365. A million minutes is almost two years. The other three are true.
hintText: Every line can be checked with a few multiplications.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A real moth once got stuck in a computer|The first webcam watched a coffee pot|The first computer mouse was made of wood|The @ sign was invented for email
explanation: The @ sign is hundreds of years old. Traders used it for prices long before it was first put into an email address in 1971. The other three are true.
hintText: The signs on a keyboard are often much older than the keyboard.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: A polar bear has black skin|A flamingo chick is grey or white, not pink|A chameleon changes colour mostly to hide|A zebra has black skin under its stripes
explanation: A chameleon changes colour mostly to show its mood, to send signals and to warm up or cool down. The other three are true.
hintText: Think of an animal that wants a rival to see it.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Moon footprints can last millions of years|Saturn is lighter than water, size for size|Summer is warm because the Sun is closer|Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet
explanation: Summer comes from the tilt of the Earth. In fact the Earth is nearest to the Sun in early January, when it is winter in the north. The other three are true.
hintText: When it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Your left lung is smaller than your right|You make about a litre of spit a day|The picture inside your eye is upside down|The blood in your veins is blue
explanation: Blood is always red. It is darker when it carries less oxygen. Veins only look blue through the skin. The other three are true.
hintText: Think of the colour you have seen with your own eyes.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops|A cloud can weigh as much as 100 elephants|Every snowflake has eight arms|Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
explanation: A snowflake has six arms or six sides, because of the way water freezes into crystals. The other three are true.
hintText: Picture a snowflake and count.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Bubble wrap was invented as wallpaper|Bicycles are older than steam locomotives|The tin can is older than the can opener|The lighter is older than the friction match
explanation: The first steam locomotive ran in 1804. The first two-wheeler, with no pedals yet, came in 1817. The other three are true.
hintText: A thing that looks simple is not always the older one.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: 'Alphabet' is named after two Greek letters|The word 'robot' comes from a Czech play|'Planet' is an old word for 'round'|The = sign was invented in the 1500s
explanation: 'Planet' comes from the Greek for 'wanderer': the planets move among the fixed stars. The other three are true.
hintText: Ask what people saw in the night sky long before they knew the shape of anything in it.

question: Three of these are true. I made one up. Which one?
optionsString: Bamboo can grow almost a metre in a day|A sunflower head is many tiny flowers|Some living trees are older than the pyramids|A mushroom is a kind of plant
explanation: Mushrooms are fungi, a group of their own. Fungi are closer relatives of animals than of plants. The other three are true.
hintText: A plant makes its food from light. Do all four need light?

question: Which is the oldest?
optionsString: Trees|Sharks|Dinosaurs|Flowers
explanation: Sharks have been around for more than 400 million years. The first trees came later, about 385 million years ago, dinosaurs and flowers long after that.
hintText: Life began in the sea.

question: Which is the largest number?
optionsString: The people on Earth|The days since the last dinosaurs|The trees on Earth|The stars in our galaxy
explanation: The Earth has about 3 trillion trees. Our galaxy has 100 to 400 billion stars. About 24 billion days have passed since the dinosaurs died out, and there are about 8 billion people.
hintText: The dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. That one can be worked out.

question: Which planet has the hottest surface?
optionsString: Mars|Mercury|Venus|Earth
explanation: Venus is the hottest, at about 465 °C, though Mercury is nearer to the Sun. The thick air of Venus holds the heat like a blanket.
hintText: Nearest to the fire is not always warmest. Think of a blanket.

question: Cleopatra lived closer in time to which of these?
optionsString: The first writing|The first Moon landing|The building of the Great Pyramid|The first farmers
explanation: Cleopatra died about 2,000 years before the Moon landing of 1969. The Great Pyramid was already about 2,500 years old when she was born.
hintText: The pyramids were ancient even for the ancient Egyptians.

question: Where does sound travel fastest?
optionsString: Through water|Through steel|Through empty space|Through air
explanation: Sound moves at about 340 m/s in air, 1,500 m/s in water and almost 6,000 m/s in steel. Stiff, tightly bound matter passes it on faster. In empty space there is no sound at all.
hintText: Sound is passed on from particle to particle. Where are they bound most tightly?

question: Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to which of these?
optionsString: Stegosaurus|The first fish|The first dinosaurs|People today
explanation: T. rex died out 66 million years ago. Stegosaurus had lived about 150 million years ago, some 80 million years before T. rex.
hintText: The age of the dinosaurs lasted far longer than the time since it ended.

question: Which organ of the body is the heaviest?
optionsString: The liver|The heart|The brain|The skin
explanation: The skin of an adult weighs about 4 kg. The liver, the heaviest organ inside the body, weighs about 1.5 kg, the brain a little less.
hintText: An organ does not have to be inside the body.

question: Mount Everest is set down in the deepest place in the sea. Where is its top?
optionsString: About 2 km above the water|About 2 km under water|About 5 km above the water|Just at the surface
explanation: Mount Everest is 8,849 m high. The deepest place in the sea, in the Pacific, is almost 11,000 m deep.
hintText: Everest is almost 9 km high. How deep can a sea be?

question: On the usual flat map Greenland looks as big as Africa. What is true?
optionsString: Africa is about twice as big|Greenland is a little bigger|They are about the same size|Africa is about 14 times bigger
explanation: Africa is about 30 million km², Greenland a little over 2 million. The usual flat map stretches the lands near the poles.
hintText: A round Earth cannot be drawn flat without stretching. Where is the stretch biggest?

question: When the Great Pyramid was built, which of these still walked the Earth?
optionsString: Neanderthals|Tyrannosaurus rex|Sabre-toothed cats|Woolly mammoths
explanation: The last woolly mammoths lived on an Arctic island until about 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid was then already more than 500 years old.
hintText: One of these animals died out much later than the others.

question: Two buckets of the same size are full to the brim: one with water, one with solid ice. Which is heavier?
optionsString: Both weigh the same|The one with water|The one with ice|It depends on how cold the ice is
explanation: Ice is about a tenth lighter than the same bucketful of water, because water swells when it freezes. That is why ice floats.
hintText: Which of the two floats on the other?

question: Which of these numbers is the largest?
optionsString: The stars in the visible universe|The drops of water in the sea|The ways to order 52 playing cards|The grains of sand on Earth
explanation: A deck of 52 cards can be ordered in 52 × 51 × 50 × … × 1 ways. That number has 68 digits. It is far larger than the number of all the sand grains, stars or drops.
hintText: For the first card there are 52 choices, for the next 51, and so on. They multiply.

question: An adult's brain is about 2 % of the body's weight. How much of the body's energy does it use?
optionsString: About 2 %|About 5 %|About 50 %|About 20 %
explanation: The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy, ten times its share of the weight. It works day and night.
hintText: The brain never rests, even in sleep. But the muscles, the heart and the gut need energy too.

question: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water?
optionsString: In clouds and rain|In plants and animals|In ice|In rivers and lakes
explanation: About two thirds of all fresh water is frozen in the ice of Antarctica and Greenland and in glaciers. Most of the rest is under the ground. Rivers and lakes hold less than 1 %.
hintText: Think of the two great white places on a globe.

question: The Moon is about 3,500 km across. Which of these is wider than the Moon?
optionsString: Greenland, from north to south|Pluto, from side to side|Australia, from west to east|India, from north to south
explanation: Australia is about 4,000 km wide. India is about 3,200 km long, Greenland about 2,700 km, and Pluto is 2,377 km across.
hintText: Three of the four can be compared on a globe.

question: Which was invented first?
optionsString: The fax machine|The aeroplane|The telephone|The radio
explanation: A machine that sent pictures along a wire was patented in 1843. The telephone came in 1876, the radio in the 1890s and the aeroplane in 1903.
hintText: To send a drawing along a wire is simpler than to send a voice.

question: Which appeared on Earth first: chickens or eggs?
optionsString: Both at the same time|Eggs|Nobody can ever know|Chickens
explanation: Fish and dinosaurs laid eggs hundreds of millions of years before the first chicken.
hintText: The question does not say which animal laid them.

question: Which is the strongest for its weight?
optionsString: Steel|Brick|Concrete|Spider silk
explanation: Spider silk is about as strong as steel, but six times lighter. So for the same weight it holds far more.
hintText: One of these has to hold a struggling fly and still weigh almost nothing.

question: Which of these birds lays the biggest egg for the size of its body?
optionsString: The ostrich|The eagle|The hen|The kiwi
explanation: A kiwi's egg is up to a fifth of the mother's weight. The ostrich lays the biggest egg of all, but it is small next to the ostrich.
hintText: Biggest for its size is not the same as biggest.

question: Which planet is, on average, the nearest to the Earth?
optionsString: Mars|Venus|Jupiter|Mercury
explanation: Venus comes closest, but it spends a long time on the far side of the Sun. Mercury stays near the Sun, so on average it is the nearest planet to the Earth, and to every other planet.
hintText: To come closest and to be nearest on average are two different things.

question: About how many times does a heart beat in one day?
optionsString: 100,000 times|10,000 times|1,000 times|1,000,000 times
explanation: About 70 beats a minute for 1,440 minutes is close to 100,000. The heart never takes a day off.
hintText: Count the beats in a minute first. A day has 1,440 minutes.

question: About how many breaths does a person take in one day?
optionsString: About 20,000|About 200,000|About 200|About 2,000
explanation: About 15 breaths a minute for 1,440 minutes is a little over 20,000.
hintText: Count your breaths for half a minute. A day has 1,440 minutes.

question: About how many Earths would fit side by side across the Sun?
optionsString: About 1,000|About 10|About 10,000|About 100
explanation: The Sun is about 1.4 million km wide and the Earth about 12,700 km. That makes 109 Earths in a row.
hintText: The Sun is about 1.4 million km wide. How wide is the Earth?

question: Light travels 300,000 km in a second. The Sun is 150 million km away. About how long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
optionsString: 8 days|8 seconds|8 minutes|8 hours
explanation: 150 million km at 300,000 km a second takes about 500 seconds. The Sun in the sky is the Sun of 8 minutes ago.
hintText: Divide the distance by the speed. A minute has 60 seconds.

question: About how many days old is a child on their 10th birthday?
optionsString: 365,000 days|365 days|36,500 days|3,650 days
explanation: Ten years of 365 days is 3,650 days, plus two or three leap days. A person turns 10,000 days old at the age of 27.
hintText: A year has 365 days.

question: About how fast does the Earth carry everyone around the Sun?
explanation: The Earth travels about 940 million km in a year of 8,766 hours. That is about 107,000 km/h, and nobody feels it.
hintText: One trip around the Sun is about 940 million km and takes a year.

question: About how much blood is in the body of an adult?
optionsString: 500 litres|5 litres|50 litres|Half a litre
explanation: An adult has about 5 litres of blood, about a thirteenth of the body's weight.
hintText: A litre of blood weighs about a kilogram. How heavy is a whole adult?

question: About how many times does a person blink in one day?
optionsString: 150,000 times|15,000 times|1,500 times|150 times
explanation: A person blinks 15 to 20 times a minute and is awake for about 16 hours. That makes about 15,000 blinks or more.
hintText: Count your blinks for ten seconds. A day awake is about 1,000 minutes.

question: A person counts one number every second, with no breaks. About how long does it take to reach a million?
optionsString: About 3 hours|About 12 days|About 30 years|About 3 years
explanation: A day has 86,400 seconds, so a million seconds is 11 and a half days. In truth it takes longer: a big number takes more than a second to say.
hintText: A day has 86,400 seconds.

question: About how far away is the Moon?
explanation: The Moon is about 384,000 km away. Light needs a little over one second for the trip.
hintText: The Earth is 40,000 km around. The Moon is much farther away than one trip around the Earth.

question: About how many times could light go around the Earth in one second?
optionsString: Less than once|About 70,000 times|About 700 times|About 7 times
explanation: Light covers about 300,000 km in a second. The Earth is 40,000 km around. 300,000 ÷ 40,000 is 7.5.
hintText: The Earth is 40,000 km around. How far does light go in a second?

question: About how many times does a bee beat its wings in one second?
optionsString: About 200|About 20|About 2|About 2,000
explanation: A honeybee beats its wings about 230 times a second. The hum is the sound of the wings.
hintText: The wings make the hum. A slow beat would make no tone at all.

question: On a clear dark night far from any town, about how many stars can a person see with bare eyes?
optionsString: About 300|About 3 billion|About 3 million|About 3,000
explanation: Only a few thousand stars, about 3,000, are bright enough to be seen at one time. The sky looks fuller than it is.
hintText: Long ago people listed every star the eye can see. Could they have listed millions?

question: A cubic metre of air weighs a little over 1 kg. A room is 4 m wide, 5 m long and 2.5 m high. About how much does the air in it weigh?
optionsString: 60 grams|6 kilograms|60 kilograms|600 grams
explanation: The room holds 50 cubic metres of air, and each one weighs about 1.2 kg. That is 60 kg, as much as a grown person.
hintText: Find how many cubic metres the room holds.

question: A Full HD screen is 1,920 dots wide and 1,080 dots high. About how many dots is that?
optionsString: 200 thousand|20 thousand|2 million|2 thousand
explanation: 1,920 × 1,080 is 2,073,600 dots. On most screens each dot is made of three tiny lights: red, green and blue.
hintText: Round both numbers before you multiply.

question: People say lightning never strikes the same place twice. Does it?
optionsString: Only at sea|Never|Yes, often|Only in the mountains
explanation: Lightning likes tall things and comes back to them. One skyscraper in New York is hit more than 20 times a year.
hintText: Lightning takes the shortest way down. Does a tall tower move away after a strike?

question: People say the Moon pulls the sea up and makes the tides. Is that right?
optionsString: No, the tides come from rivers|Yes, mostly the Moon does it|No, the turning Earth alone does|No, the wind makes the tides
explanation: The pull of the Moon raises the sea on the side that faces it and on the far side. The Sun helps a little, with less than half the Moon's effect.
hintText: High tide comes about 50 minutes later each day. What else in the sky does that?

question: People say a goldfish forgets everything after three seconds. How long can it remember?
optionsString: About a minute|For months|About three seconds|About an hour
explanation: A goldfish can learn where and when it is fed and still know it months later.
hintText: A fish that forgot everything at once could not learn where its food comes from.

question: People say the colour red makes a bull angry. What makes it charge?
optionsString: The smell of the cloth|The colour red|The moving cloth|The shine of the cloth
explanation: A bull can hardly tell red from green. It is the waving that makes it charge. A cloth of any colour works.
hintText: Cattle see fewer colours than people do.

question: Can the Great Wall of China be seen from the Moon with bare eyes?
optionsString: No, it is far too narrow|No, clouds always hide it|Yes, but only at night|Yes, as a thin line
explanation: The wall is very long but only a few metres wide. From the Moon the whole Earth can be hidden behind a thumb.
hintText: Long is not enough to be seen. How wide is a wall?

question: People say we use only a tenth of our brain. How much do we really use?
optionsString: Nearly all of it|About a tenth|About a quarter|About half
explanation: Over a day nearly every part of the brain is active, and much of it even in sleep. No part sits unused.
hintText: The brain needs a lot of the body's energy. Would a body feed something it does not use?

question: What does a camel store in its hump?
optionsString: Fat|Milk|Water|Air
explanation: The hump is a store of fat for weeks without food. A thirsty camel can drink about 100 litres in one go, but that water does not go to the hump.
hintText: The hump gets small and floppy when a camel has not eaten for a long time.

question: People say a rainbow is really a full circle. Is it?
optionsString: Only when it rains over the sea|No, it is always half a circle|Yes, the ground hides the lower part|No, it is a flat band of light
explanation: A rainbow is a circle of light around the point opposite the Sun. From the ground only the upper part has room to show. From a plane the whole circle can be seen.
hintText: Think of where the raindrops are missing when someone stands on the ground.

question: People say we have five senses. How many do we really have?
optionsString: More than five|Exactly five|Four|Three
explanation: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, the body senses balance, warmth and cold, and pain.
hintText: Which sense says that you are upside down when your eyes are closed?

question: Does a banana grow on a tree?
optionsString: Yes, on a palm tree|No, on a climbing vine|Yes, on a low bushy tree|No, on a giant plant with no wood
explanation: A banana plant has no wood. Its 'trunk' is made of tightly rolled leaves. Banana plants are among the largest herbs in the world.
hintText: A tree has a trunk of wood. Not every tall plant has one.

question: In pictures the Sun is yellow. What colour is sunlight above the air, out in space?
optionsString: Red|Orange|Yellow|White
explanation: Sunlight is a mix of all colours, and that mix is white. The air scatters some of the blue away, so from the ground the Sun looks yellowish.
hintText: What colour are clouds and snow in sunlight?

question: People say water goes down the drain the other way round south of the equator. Does it?
optionsString: Yes, but only in baths|No, the shape of the basin decides|Only on the equator itself|Yes, always
explanation: The turning of the Earth steers huge storms, but it is far too weak for a sink. There the shape of the basin and the last push on the water decide.
hintText: The Earth turns once a day. How much is that in the few seconds a sink needs?

question: People say dogs see only black and white. What do they see?
optionsString: Only black, white and grey|All the colours we see|Only red and green|Blue and yellow, but not red
explanation: A dog's eye has two kinds of colour cells, ours has three. Dogs see blues and yellows well. Red looks dark and brownish to them.
hintText: Two kinds of colour cells are fewer than three, but more than none.

question: Mount Everest reaches highest above the sea. Which mountain is the tallest from its foot to its top?
optionsString: Mauna Kea in Hawaii|Mont Blanc in Europe|Kilimanjaro in Africa|Mount Everest again
explanation: Mauna Kea stands on the sea floor. From foot to top it is about 10,000 m tall, but only some 4,200 m of it are above the water.
hintText: A mountain's foot does not have to be on dry land.

question: People say Columbus proved that the Earth is round. When did learned people really find out?
optionsString: With the first telescope, in 1608|With the first photo from space|In ancient Greece, over 2,000 years ago|When Columbus sailed, in 1492
explanation: The Greeks had measured the round Earth about 2,200 years ago, and scholars of the Middle Ages taught it. Columbus and his critics argued only about how big the globe was.
hintText: The Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round. People saw that long ago.

question: Which of these is a berry to a plant scientist?
optionsString: Strawberry|Cherry|Banana|Raspberry
explanation: To a plant scientist a berry is one soft fruit with its seeds in the flesh and no hard stone. That fits a banana, a grape and a tomato. A cherry has a stone, a raspberry is many tiny fruits, and a strawberry carries its seeds on the outside.
hintText: Look where each one has its seeds.

question: A fruit is the part of a plant that holds its seeds. Which of these is not a fruit?
optionsString: Pumpkin|Cucumber|Rhubarb|Sweet pepper
explanation: Cucumbers, pumpkins and peppers hold seeds, so they are fruits. Of rhubarb we eat the leaf stalk.
hintText: Three of them have seeds inside.

question: Which of these animals is a fish?
optionsString: Seahorse|Dolphin|Cuttlefish|Starfish
explanation: A seahorse has gills, fins and a backbone: a real fish. A dolphin is a mammal, and a starfish and a cuttlefish have no backbone at all.
hintText: A fish has a backbone and breathes with gills.

question: Which of these is a crustacean, like crabs and shrimps?
optionsString: Beetle|Woodlouse|Centipede|Spider
explanation: A woodlouse is a crustacean that moved onto land. It still breathes with gill-like organs, which is why it needs damp places.
hintText: Crabs breathe with gills and must stay moist. Which of the four dries out fastest?

question: Which living animal is the closest relative of the elephant?
optionsString: Hippopotamus|Manatee (sea cow)|Rhinoceros|Wild boar
explanation: Sea cows and elephants come from the same ancestors. Most manatees even have toenails on their flippers, and a manatee's teeth are replaced from behind, like an elephant's.
hintText: To look alike does not mean to be related.

question: What kind of animal is a koala?
optionsString: A relative of the bear|A relative of the squirrel|A relative of the monkey|A relative of the kangaroo
explanation: A koala carries its young in a pouch. It is no bear, though it is called one in some languages.
hintText: Think of where it lives and who its neighbours are.

question: What is a coral?
optionsString: A rock|An animal|A plant|A seaweed
explanation: A coral is a colony of tiny animals, relatives of jellyfish. They build a hard skeleton of limestone, and that is the 'rock'.
hintText: It catches food with tiny arms.

question: People call a very bright light that often shines in the west after sunset the 'evening star'. What is it?
optionsString: A space station|The North Star|The planet Venus|A comet
explanation: The evening star is not a star. It is Venus, shining with the light of the Sun. Of all the stars and planets it looks the brightest.
hintText: It stays close to the place where the Sun went down.

question: What is a shooting star?
optionsString: A satellite catching the sunlight|A piece broken off the Moon|A grain of dust burning up in the air|A star falling out of the sky
explanation: Most shooting stars are bits of space dust about the size of a grain of sand. They hit the air so fast that they glow and burn up high above the ground.
hintText: A real star is far bigger than the Earth. Could one fall here?

question: Window glass and the glass of a screen are made mostly from what?
optionsString: Ground sea shells|Melted salt|Clear plastic|Melted sand
explanation: Glass is mostly sand, melted at about 1,500 °C with some soda and lime and then cooled.
hintText: The main ingredient lies around in huge amounts and costs almost nothing.

question: The answer is 8. What was the question?
optionsString: How many wings does a bee have?|How many horns did Triceratops have?|How many legs does a bee have?|How many legs does a spider have?
explanation: A spider has 8 legs. A bee has 6 legs and 4 wings. Triceratops had 3 horns, and its name says so.
hintText: All insects have the same number of legs. A spider is not an insect.

question: The answer is 2. What was the question?
optionsString: How many moons does Mars have?|How many moons does the Earth have?|How many moons does Mercury have?|How many moons does Venus have?
explanation: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. The Earth has one. Venus and Mercury have none.
hintText: One of these can be answered by a look at the night sky.

question: The answer is 32. What was the question?
optionsString: How many milk teeth does a child have?|How many ribs does a person have?|How many bones are in one hand?|How many teeth are in a full adult set?
explanation: An adult has 32 teeth with the four wisdom teeth. A child has 20 milk teeth. A hand has 27 bones, and a person has 24 ribs.
hintText: One of these can be counted with the tip of the tongue.

question: The answer is 0. What was the question?
optionsString: How many wings does a dragonfly have?|How many legs does a lobster have?|How many toes are on an ostrich's foot?|How many bones does a shark have?
explanation: A shark's skeleton is cartilage, the bendy stuff of ears and noses. An ostrich has 2 toes on each foot, a lobster 10 legs and a dragonfly 4 wings.
hintText: A foot has toes, and a thing that flies has wings. So look at the other two.

question: The answer is 5. What was the question?
optionsString: How many wings does a fly have?|How many eyes does a bee have?|How many eyes do most spiders have?|How many legs does a butterfly have?
explanation: A bee has two big eyes and three small ones on top of its head. A fly has 2 wings, a butterfly 6 legs, and most spiders have 8 eyes.
hintText: Legs and wings come in pairs. Can a number of pairs be 5?

question: The answer is 4. What was the question?
optionsString: How many long bones are in one arm?|How many pairs of ribs does a person have?|How many chambers does the heart have?|How many tiny bones are in one ear?
explanation: The heart has four chambers. Each ear has 3 tiny bones, the smallest in the body. An arm has 3 long bones, one above the elbow and two below, and a person has 12 pairs of ribs.
hintText: The heart has a left and a right half, and each half has an upper and a lower part.

question: The answer is Mars. What was the question?
optionsString: Which planet lies on its side?|Which planet has the fastest winds?|Which planet is the smallest?|Which planet has the tallest volcano?
explanation: Olympus Mons on Mars is more than 21 km high, more than twice Mount Everest. The smallest planet is Mercury, Uranus lies on its side, and Neptune has the fastest winds.
hintText: Mars is a small rocky world, but not the smallest, and its air is thin.

question: The answer is orange. What was the question?
optionsString: What colour does copper turn in the rain?|What colour is a sunset on Mars?|What colour is the Moon's sky by day?|What colour is a plane's 'black box'?
explanation: A flight recorder is bright orange, so that it is easy to find. A sunset on Mars is blue, old copper turns green, and the Moon's sky is black even by day.
hintText: A thing that must be found fast needs a colour that stands out.

question: The answer is 64. What was the question?
optionsString: How many dots are on one die?|How many squares are on a chessboard?|How many patches are on a classic football?|How many keys does a piano have?
explanation: A chessboard has 8 × 8 = 64 squares. A piano has 88 keys, a classic football is sewn from 32 patches, and the dots on a die add up to 21.
hintText: One of the four can be worked out with one multiplication.

question: The answer is Arabic. What was the question?
optionsString: Which language gave us the word 'tsunami'?|Which language gave us the word 'algebra'?|Which language gave us the word 'yoghurt'?|Which language gave us the word 'piano'?
explanation: 'Algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr', from the title of a maths book written about 1,200 years ago. 'Tsunami' is Japanese, 'piano' Italian and 'yoghurt' Turkish.
hintText: Many old words of maths and many star names came to Europe from one language.

question: Try it: close your mouth, pinch your nose shut and hum very softly. What happens?
optionsString: The hum gets louder|The hum stops after a moment|The hum gets higher|Nothing changes
explanation: A hum sends air out through the nose. With the nose shut the air has nowhere to go.
hintText: The quickest way to know is to do it.

question: Try it: lay a hand flat on your leg and fold the middle finger under. Now lift the other fingers one at a time. Which one stays down?
optionsString: The little finger|The thumb|The index finger|The ring finger
explanation: The tendons that lift the ring finger and the middle finger are tied together. When one finger is held down, the other is stuck.
hintText: Do it, one finger after the other.

question: Try it: hold a hand a little away from your mouth. Breathe on it with the mouth wide open, then blow through tight lips. What do you feel?
optionsString: Wide is warm, tight is cool|Both feel warm|Both feel cool|Wide is cool, tight is warm
explanation: The breath is equally warm both times. A thin fast stream pulls cooler room air along and dries the skin, and that feels cool.
hintText: Your hand is the measuring tool. Use it.

question: Try it: hold a thumb up at arm's length. Look at it with one eye, then with the other. What does the thumb do?
optionsString: It jumps sideways|It stays where it is|It gets bigger|It changes colour
explanation: Each eye looks from its own place, a few centimetres from the other. The brain uses the difference between the two pictures to judge how far away things are.
hintText: Close the left eye, then the right. Watch what is behind the thumb.

question: Try it: put two fingers on your throat. Hum softly, then whisper. When does the throat buzz?
optionsString: Both times|Only when humming|Only when whispering|Neither time
explanation: A voice is made by two small folds in the throat that shake. In a whisper they stay still and only air goes through.
hintText: Your fingers will tell you.

question: Try it: close one eye and look straight ahead. What is always at the edge of the picture?
optionsString: Your own nose|A second picture|A black spot|Nothing at all
explanation: The nose is always in view. The brain just leaves it out, because it never changes. Now you will see it for a while.
hintText: Look towards the middle of your face without turning the head.

question: Try it: press on a fingernail for three seconds, then let go and watch the nail. What happens?
optionsString: It is pale, then pink again|It turns blue for a while|It is dark, then pale again|It keeps its colour
explanation: The press pushes the blood out of the tiny vessels under the nail. When the finger lets go, the blood is back in about two seconds.
hintText: Watch the colour under the nail at the moment the finger lets go.

question: Try it: close your eyes and touch the tip of your nose with a finger. How did the finger find the way?
optionsString: By a sense for where your limbs are|By the sense of balance|By remembering the last try|By feeling the air on the skin
explanation: Sensors in the muscles and joints tell the brain where every part of the body is, with no need to look. It works in the dark and under a blanket too.
hintText: You did not see, hear or smell your hand. Something else told you where it was.

question: How much of an iceberg is hidden under the water?
optionsString: About nine tenths|About a tenth|Almost none|About half
explanation: Ice is only a little lighter than sea water, so an iceberg floats with about 90 % of itself below the surface.
hintText: Ice floats, but only just.

question: What does the word 'dinosaur' mean?
optionsString: Giant bird|Old dragon|Terrible lizard|Thunder beast
explanation: The name was made in 1842 from two Greek words: 'deinos', terrible, and 'sauros', lizard.
hintText: The second half, 'saur', turns up in the names of many of these animals.

question: Long before machines, what was a 'computer'?
optionsString: A person who did sums as a job|A board with counting beads|A part of a clock|A book of number tables
explanation: For about 300 years a computer was a person paid to calculate, often in a room full of others. The machines took over the name.
hintText: To compute means to calculate. Who did that before machines?

question: When in the day is a person tallest?
optionsString: The same all day|After lunch|In the evening|In the morning
explanation: The soft discs between the bones of the back are pressed together a little during the day. In the evening a person is 1 to 2 cm shorter. Lying down at night lets the discs fill up again.
hintText: Think of what a day of standing and sitting does to a stack of soft cushions.

question: How does a phone screen feel a finger?
optionsString: The finger warms the glass|A camera under the glass sees it|The finger presses the glass down|The finger changes an electric field
explanation: The screen holds a weak electric field. Skin conducts electricity and changes the field where it touches. That is why a normal glove or a plastic pen does not work.
hintText: It works with the lightest touch, but not through a thick glove.

question: How does a phone know which way up it is held?
optionsString: It listens for echoes|The camera looks at the room|It measures the light on each side|A tiny sensor feels the pull of gravity
explanation: A chip smaller than a grain of rice holds a tiny weight on springs. Gravity pulls the weight down, and the phone reads which way 'down' is.
hintText: It works in the dark and in silence.

question: How does a phone find its place on a map?
optionsString: Satellites take pictures of it|It times signals from satellites|It feels the Earth's magnetic field|It counts steps from home
explanation: Each navigation satellite sends the exact time. The phone compares how late the signals from four or more of them arrive, and works out where it must be.
hintText: The satellites only send. They do not know that the phone exists.
